prompt.context: Your client is a satellite television service provider. Recently, the client has been experiencing declining revenues and market share because of increased competition from cable-based television providers. Cable-based providers offer a range of services including phone, internet and television (commonly called a 'triple play'). Our client currently only offers television services and has been losing customers to competitors offering triple play services. Our client is exploring the possibility of expanding services to include a bundled phone and internet package.
prompt.question: Should the client expand its service offerings to include a bundled phone and internet package? Walk through your analysis.

clarifying_info.q: Will the satellite television business be affected?
clarifying_info.a: No, the satellite television broadcast and business will stay unchanged.

clarifying_info.q: How will phone service be delivered?
clarifying_info.a: Phone service will be conducted via Voice over IP (VOIP) requiring access to broadband towers.

clarifying_info.q: What equipment does each customer need?
clarifying_info.a: Each customer needs one receiver box for television (current customers already have this) and a separate box for phone and internet.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market position?
clarifying_info.a: There are only three major players in the television market; the client is #3 with 20% market share and a market cap of $3B.

exhibits.title: Internet and Phone Infrastructure
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the infrastructure required to deliver broadband internet and phone (VOIP) services, including towers, spectrum, and in-home equipment (CPE box).
exhibits.data: Three key infrastructure inputs labeled: (1) Towers, (2) Spectrum, (3) In-home box / CPE (Client Premise Equipment)

exhibits.title: Auction Price Spectrum
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the average auction price for broadband spectrum across 12 auctions (numbered 1-12), with prices ranging from approximately $200M to $1,200M.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: Average Auction Price BB Spectrum (Millions), range 0-1400; X-axis: Auction Number 1-12; Average line marked at $500M

framework: Define the market opportunity: estimate the addressable market for triple play among existing and new customers
Quantify revenues: derive annual revenue from projected subscriber base and pricing
Quantify costs: identify and size capital and operating costs (towers, spectrum, CPE)
Evaluate lease vs. buy decision for tower infrastructure

questions.prompt: Determine the potential market size for the additional phone and internet bundled service.
questions.guidance: Candidate should split the market into two segments: (1) existing triple-play cable customers the client can poach, and (2) the client's own TV subscribers who can be upsold. Use the assumptions provided to build up to total addressable households.

math.setup: US Households = 100M; 50% have cable; 40% of cable customers have triple play; client captures 10% of existing triple play market; client converts 40% of its own TV subscribers to triple play.
steps: Total existing triple play market: 100M x 50% x 40% = 20M households
Client captures 10% of existing triple play: 20M x 10% = 2.0M households
Client's existing TV subscribers: 100M x 50% cable x 20% market share = 10M (note: casebook uses 50M cable x 20% = 10M, equivalent)
Convert 40% of own subscribers: 10M x 40% = 4.0M households
Total new triple play customers: 2.0M + 4.0M = 6.0M households

questions.prompt: Determine the annual revenues for the additional phone and internet bundled service.
questions.guidance: Straightforward revenue calculation; candidate should multiply total subscriber households by monthly price and annualize.

questions.prompt: Determine the annual costs for the additional phone and internet bundled service.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the three cost components: towers (lease vs. buy), spectrum, and CPE. Strong candidates note the massive capital outlay of the buy option and may comment on auction price volatility from Exhibit 2.

math.setup: 200 towers required nationwide. Tower purchase: $15M/tower + $0.2M/year maintenance. Tower lease: $2.2M/year/tower (all-in). Spectrum: average $500M (from Exhibit 2). CPE: $20/box x 6.0M households.
steps: Tower Purchase option: $15M x 200 = $3,000M capex + $0.2M x 200 = $40M/year maintenance; Total year-1 = $3,000M + $40M + $500M + $120M = $3,660M (casebook rounds to $3.7B including all)
Tower Lease option: $2.2M x 200 = $440M/year opex; Year-1 total = $500M spectrum + $120M CPE + $440M lease = $1,060M ($620M one-time capex + $440M annual opex)
math.answer: Buy towers: ~$3.7B total year-1 cost (predominantly capex). Lease towers: ~$1.06B year-1 ($620M capex + $440M annual opex).

questions.prompt: What factors should the client consider when determining whether to lease or buy towers?
questions.guidance: Candidate should produce a structured pro/con analysis. Excellent answers cover financial, operational, and strategic dimensions for both options.

questions.prompt: Determine the profitability (NPV) of the two scenarios: buy towers vs. lease towers.
questions.guidance: Candidate uses a growing-perpetuity NPV formula. Key inputs: revenue, operating costs, depreciation (non-cash, shields tax), tax rate, discount rate, growth rate. Strong candidates note that leasing yields a higher NPV despite lower control, and may discuss why buying could still be preferred (long-term cost savings, asset ownership).

math.setup: Discount rate = 15%; growth rate = 5%; tax rate = 34%; depreciation = $20M/year (equals CAPEX, no net working capital change). NPV = -Investment + FCF / (r - g) using growing perpetuity.
steps: BUY TOWERS - Investment: $3,000M towers + $500M spectrum + $120M CPE = $3,620M

BUY - Annual FCF: (Revenue $1,440M - Maintenance $40M - Depreciation $20M) x (1 - 34%) = $1,380M x 0.66 = $910.8M ≈ $910M (then add back depreciation: casebook calculates as ($1,440 - $40 - $20) x 0.66 = $910M, uses this as FCF proxy since CAPEX = Depreciation)
BUY - NPV: -$3,620M + $910M / (0.15 - 0.05) = -$3,620M + $9,100M = $5,480M (casebook shows $5,488M with slight rounding difference)
LEASE - Annual FCF: ($1,440M - $440M lease) x 0.66 = $1,000M x 0.66 = $660M
math.answer: Buy NPV ≈ $5,488M; Lease NPV ≈ $5,980M. Both are strongly positive; leasing yields a slightly higher NPV due to lower upfront investment.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the client consider when determining whether to lease or buy the towers?

categories.name: Lease Pros
ideas: Easy to exit if the venture is not profitable
No need to build tower maintenance and operations expertise internally

categories.name: Lease Cons
ideas: Subject to rising lease prices over time
Less control over service levels and uptime
Ultimately less profitable in the long run

categories.name: Buy Pros
ideas: Full control over infrastructure and service levels
Lower long-run costs once capex is amortized
Asset can be monetized (e.g., leased to third parties)

categories.name: Buy Cons
ideas: Requires building maintenance and operations expertise
Difficult to exit or right-size if demand is lower than expected

recommendation: The client should enter the triple-play market; both NPV scenarios (buy: ~$5.5B, lease: ~$6.0B) are strongly positive against the current market cap of $3B.
If entering, leasing towers is the preferred initial strategy: it minimizes upfront capital risk ($620M vs. $3.6B), preserves flexibility to exit, and actually yields a higher NPV.
Strong candidates may recommend buying towers for long-term value creation while acknowledging the capital risk, and suggest hybrid approaches or staged build-out.
risks: Auction price volatility for spectrum could significantly raise costs (Exhibit 2 shows range of ~$200M–$1,200M vs. $500M average)
Execution risk: building a new technology stack (VOIP, broadband) is operationally complex for a satellite TV company
Competitive response from incumbent triple-play providers (cable companies) could erode projected 10% market capture
CPE rollout logistics for 6M households is a significant operational undertaking
If leasing, tower lessors may raise prices or renegotiate terms as the client becomes dependent
next_steps: Conduct spectrum auction due diligence and model sensitivity to auction prices
Evaluate potential technology or operational partnerships to reduce build risk
Pilot the triple-play bundle in one or two metro markets before national rollout
Analyze customer retention impact on existing satellite TV subscriber base
Develop a detailed capital allocation plan comparing lease vs. buy at different demand scenarios
